questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How journalists stay safe in dangerous countries
How war affects children, through a reporter's experience
Why children have nightmares after watching the news
How schools teach children about history
questions.why: They talk about how war affects children, hearing from war reporter Fergal Keane.

questions.q: According to the 2024 figure, how many children live in conflict zones?
options: About one in ten children worldwide
About half of all children
About one in every five children worldwide
About 52 million children
questions.why: Becca says 520 million children live in conflict zones, about one in every five.

questions.q: What happened to Fergal Keane as a result of reporting from war zones?
options: He developed a stress disorder
He decided to stop working as a journalist
He started a charity for children
He was badly injured
questions.why: Neil says Fergal developed PTSD, a type of stress disorder, as a result of his reporting.

questions.q: Why was Fergal very watchful for danger from an early age?
options: He grew up in a war zone in another country
His parents were both soldiers in the army
He often got lost in big cities as a child
He grew up at home with an alcoholic father
questions.why: He grew up with an alcoholic father and was always checking whether he was under threat.

questions.q: What do researchers all agree on, according to Fergal?
options: Children in war zones are doing better than before
Children can't recover while the trauma continues
Children recover faster than adults in every case
Children should never talk about the war at all
questions.why: He says they're 'of one mind' that you can't recover from war trauma with continuing trauma.

questions.q: What does the new theory encourage traumatised children to do?
options: Slowly face simple challenges, like sleeping alone
Talk about the war in detail every single day
Move to another, safer country immediately
Try hard to forget everything that happened
questions.why: Fergal says it encourages children to slowly confront things like sleeping alone, without a parent.

questions.q: Why does Fergal mention putting to bed a child who has had a nightmare?
options: To show that nightmares are the main cause of trauma
To explain why children in war zones sleep well
To give advice to parents about bedtime
To show that learning to sleep alone is harder than it sounds
questions.why: He says it sounds simple, but anyone who's settled a child after a nightmare knows it's very difficult.

questions.q: What is the 'big lesson' Fergal has learned from his reporting?
options: Children usually forget difficult experiences quickly
Most children never recover from war
Given a chance, children are extremely good at recovering
Adults are stronger than children
questions.why: He says given a chance, the human spirit, especially children, is 'phenomenally resilient'.
